question: What must an internal audit department assess when it reviews its own risk-based audit work?
expected: Whether that auditing actually reduced the risks. Where the real risk profile differs from what the plan assumed, that gap must be examined to test whether the risk-assessment method is sound.
predicted: When an internal audit department reviews its own risk‑based audit work it must use the risk assessment to focus on the material risk areas and to prioritise the audit work. The assessment must include identification of the inherent business risks in the activities undertaken, evaluation of how effective the control systems are for monitoring those risks (control risk), and the preparation of a risk‑matrix covering both inherent and control risks. It must also clearly spell out how the level (high, medium, low) and trend (increasing, stable, decreasing) of those risks are determined, and may employ both quantitative and qualitative approaches in the assessment.

citations.quote: The risk assessment in the Internal Audit department should be used for focusing on the material risk areas and prioritising the audit work.

The risk assessment process should, inter alia, include identification of inherent business risks in various activities undertaken, evaluation of the effectiveness of the control systems for monitoring the inherent risks of the business activities (‘Control risk’) and drawing-up a risk-matrix for both the factors viz., inherent business risks and control risks.
The basis for determination of the level (high, medium, low) and trend (increasing, stable, decreasing) of inherent business risks and control risks should be clearly spelt out.

The risk assessment may make use of both quantitative and qualitative approaches. While the quantum of credit, market, and operational risks could largely be determined by quantitative assessment, the qualitative approach may be adopted for assessing the quality of overall governance and controls in various business activities.

2. These Directions are being issued in exercise of powers conferred by sections 21, 35A and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, sections 45JA, 45L and 45M of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and section 6 of the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011.

question: On 29 April 2026 an amendment to the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions triggered a consequential amendment to another rulebook. Which rulebook, and did this happen for more than one type of institution?
expected:
The Responsible Business Conduct Directions. On 29 April 2026 RBI issued
Responsible Business Conduct Amendment Directions for both Non-Banking
Financial Companies (RBI/2026-27/70) and Local Area Banks (RBI/2026-27/54),
each issued as a consequence of that institution's own Resolution of
Stressed Assets Amendment Directions of the same date. The cascade pattern
is identical for both; only the institution and the enabling statutes differ
- NBFCs under the RBI Act 1934, National Housing Bank Act 1987 and Factoring
Regulation Act 2011, Local Area Banks under the Banking Regulation Act 1949.
predicted: The amendment to the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions on 29 April 2026 triggered a consequential amendment to the Credit Risk Management rulebook. This occurred for more than one type of institution – it was done for both Non‑Banking Financial Companies and All India Financial Institutions.

citations.quote: Please refer to Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 dated April 29, 2026.
Please refer to Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Amendment Directions, 2026 dated April 29, 2026 .

question: Do banks normally deal in property?
expected: Banks don't normally deal in property, except when they seize it from a defaulter.
predicted: Yes. Commercial banks routinely engage with real‑estate assets, for example by accepting properties as collateral for loans and by maintaining valuation policies for such properties. The directions require banks to have a policy for valuation of properties accepted as security and to value them conservatively. They may also treat revalued property as part of CET1 capital subject to conditions. Additionally, the directions describe how banks may have absolute or pari‑passu claims over the property used as security.

citations.quote: Value of the property: Banks shall put in place a policy for valuation of properties accepted as security for their exposures. The valuation shall be appraised independently using prudently conservative valuation criteria.
property consequent upon its revaluation may be reckoned as CET1 capital at a discount of 55 per cent, subject to meeting the following conditions:

Claims over the property: A single bank has an absolute claim or multiple banks have first pari-passu claims over the property, subject to the condition that: (a) there is an inter-creditor agreement or any other arrangements among the banks detailing the sequence of claims of individual banks over the property, (b) each bank’s loan should be fully secured by the current value of the property, either as primary security or as collateral or both, and is within the permissible LTV limit, failing which risk weights under Table 16 or 17, as applicable, shall apply.

question: What does Urban Co-operative Banks capital adequacy amendment state?
expected:
Not answerable from this source. The chunk points to the methodology for
computing Net Open Position and the foreign-exchange capital charge as set
out in other documents, without stating the amendment's own content.
predicted: The Third Amendment Directions, 2026 for Urban Co-operative Banks revise the Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy by substituting sub‑paragraph 20(18) of the 2025 Directions with new wording. The amendment is issued under the name “Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Third Amendment Directions, 2026” and will become effective on 1 April 2027. It was introduced to ensure consistent implementation of the methodology for computing Net Open Position and the capital charge on foreign‑exchange risk across Urban Co‑operative Banks.

citations.quote: These instructions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Third Amendment Directions, 2026.

Upon a review and to ensure consistent implementation across Urban Co-operative Banks, there is a felt need to amend these instructions.

question: What is The Housing Finance Companies Second Amendment about and when does it become effective?
expected: The Housing Finance Companies Second Amendment, effective 1 January 2027, deletes the old advertising/marketing/sales and DSA-DMA code sub-sections from the Fair Practices Code chapter and replaces them with a new combined sub-section on advertising, marketing and sale of financial products.
predicted: The Second Amendment Directions for Housing Finance Companies revise the Fair Practices Code: the earlier sub‑sections A.10 (Advertising, Marketing and Sales) and A.11 (Code of Conduct for DSAs/DMAs) are deleted and replaced by a new sub‑section A.11A that requires HFCs to comply with paragraphs 101A to 101ZA of the RBI (Non‑Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025. The amendment comes into force on 1 January 2027.

citations.quote: (1) These Directions shall come into effect on January 1, 2027 .

(1) In Chapter‑X on ‘Fair Practices Code’, the sub‑sections A.10 Advertising, Marketing and Sales (paragraphs 150 to 154) and A.11 Code of Conduct for DSAs/DMAs (paragraphs 155 to 157) shall be deleted and substituted with a new sub‑section as under:
“A.11A Advertising, Marketing and Sale of Financial Products / Services by HFCs
157A. An HFC shall ensure compliance with the provisions of paragraphs 101A to 101ZA under Chapter IIIA of Reserve Bank of India (Non‑Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 .”
